step.adapter.none.detail: Windows reports no usable network adapter. Check whether a network card is installed and its driver is working.
step.adapter.disabled.detail: The adapter exists but is switched off in Windows. Enable it under Network connections.
step.link.disconnected.detail: The adapter is on but has no link. The network cable is unplugged or broken, or the device at the other end is off.
step.link.wifiNotAssociated: Not connected to a Wi-Fi network
step.link.wifiNotAssociated.detail: The Wi-Fi adapter is on but not associated with an access point. Select a network, or check that you are in range.
step.ip.none.detail: The adapter has no usable IPv4 address, so no traffic can leave this machine.
step.ip.apipa.detail: This is an automatic fallback address Windows assigns itself when no DHCP server answers. Your router most likely did not hand out an address.
step.gateway.none.detail: No default gateway is configured, so nothing outside your own subnet can be reached.
step.gateway.unreachable.detail: Your router did not answer a ping or a connection attempt. It may be restarting, or something between you and it is blocking traffic.
step.publicIp.none.detail: None of the public test addresses answered. Either the connection is down, or this network blocks ping traffic.
step.dns.slow: Name resolution is slower than usual.
step.dns.failed.detail: Neither your own DNS server nor the public test resolvers answered, which points at the connection rather than at DNS itself.
step.dns.ownResolverFailed: Your DNS server is not answering
step.dns.ownResolverFailed.detail: Public resolvers answered the same question without trouble, so the problem is the DNS server this machine is configured to use.
step.target.allFailed: None of the {0} targets are reachable
step.target.serverError.detail: The server answered, but with an error - the connection is fine, the service is not.
step.latency.high: Response times are higher than usual.
step.simulated.detail: This step was forced to fail by the fault simulator. Nothing is actually wrong with it.

explain.adapter.what: Windows cannot find a usable network adapter, or the one it found is switched off.
explain.adapter.cause: The adapter ({0}) is disabled in Windows, or its driver has stopped working.
explain.adapter.todo: Open Network connections in Windows and check that the adapter is enabled. If it is missing entirely, reinstall or update its driver.
explain.link.what: The network adapter is on, but nothing is connected to it.
explain.link.cause: {0} has no link. The network cable is unplugged or broken, or the switch or router at the other end is off.
explain.link.todo: Check both ends of the network cable, and try a different cable or a different port.
explain.link.wifi.what: The Wi-Fi adapter is on, but it is not connected to a network.
explain.link.wifi.cause: {0} is not associated with any access point - typically out of range, the wrong password, or the access point being down.
explain.link.wifi.todo: Open the Wi-Fi list and reconnect to your network. If it is not listed, move closer to the access point or restart it.
explain.ipConfig.what: This computer has no usable address on the network.
explain.ipConfig.cause: The adapter has no IPv4 address ({0}), so nothing can be sent anywhere.
explain.ipConfig.todo: Check whether the network is set to obtain an address automatically, and restart the router if it hands out addresses.
explain.ipConfig.apipa.what: This computer gave itself an emergency address because no router answered.
explain.ipConfig.apipa.cause: The address {0} is in the 169.254.x.x range, which Windows assigns itself when no DHCP server replies. The router did not hand out an address.
explain.ipConfig.apipa.todo: Restart the router and wait a minute. If that does not help, disconnect and reconnect the network connection to request a new address.
explain.gateway.what: Your own router cannot be reached.
explain.gateway.cause: {0} answered neither a ping nor a connection attempt, which usually means it is restarting, has crashed, or is no longer on this network.
explain.gateway.todo: Check whether the router is on and its lights are normal. Restarting it is the usual fix; if other devices work fine, the problem is between this computer and the router.
explain.internet.what: The local network works, but nothing outside it can be reached.
explain.internet.cause: None of the {0} public test addresses answered and no site could be reached, which points at the connection between your router and your provider.
explain.internet.todo: Check whether other devices on the same network also have no internet. If they do not, restart the modem or router and check the status page of your provider.
explain.dns.what: Names cannot be turned into addresses, so sites do not open even though the connection works.
explain.dns.cause: The lookup of {0} failed, and the public test resolvers did not answer either ({1}).
explain.dns.todo: Restart the router. If the problem persists, try setting a public DNS server such as 9.9.9.9 or 1.1.1.1.
explain.dns.ownResolver.what: The DNS server this computer uses is not answering, while the rest of the connection is fine.
explain.dns.ownResolver.cause: Looking up {0} failed through your own DNS server ({1}), but public resolvers answered the same question without trouble.
explain.dns.ownResolver.todo: Set a different DNS server in your network settings, or restart the router that provides it.
explain.target.what: The connection works, but the site or service being monitored cannot be reached.
explain.target.cause: {0} did not respond, while the rest of the network checks passed.
explain.target.todo: The problem is most likely at the other end. Check whether the site works from another device or network before changing anything here.
explain.target.serverError.what: The service answers, but with an error.
explain.target.serverError.cause: {0} returned a server error. The network path is fine end to end; the service behind it is not healthy.
explain.target.serverError.todo: Nothing to fix on this side. If it persists, report it to whoever runs the service.
explain.target.tls.what: The connection is established, but the secure handshake fails.
explain.target.tls.cause: {0} failed during the TLS handshake - typically an expired or untrusted certificate, or something intercepting the connection.
explain.target.tls.todo: Check the system clock, and whether antivirus or a corporate proxy is inspecting HTTPS traffic.
explain.firewall.what: The connection works, but the test pings are being blocked.
explain.firewall.cause: Pings get no answer while real traffic goes through, so something on the way is filtering ICMP rather than the connection being down.
explain.firewall.todo: Nothing is actually broken. This is normal on corporate, hotel and some mobile networks.
explain.firewall.gateway.what: Your router does not answer pings, but traffic through it works.
explain.firewall.gateway.cause: The gateway answered neither ping nor connection attempts, yet the internet beyond it is reachable - so the router is simply configured not to reply.
explain.firewall.gateway.todo: Nothing is actually broken. Many routers hide from pings by default.
explain.unknown.what: Something is wrong, but the cause could not be narrowed down.
explain.unknown.cause: The checks did not produce a clear pattern.
explain.unknown.todo: Look at the Diagnostics page for the individual measurements.
traceroute.title: Traceroute
traceroute.subtitle: Every router between here and the target, and what each one is telling us
traceroute.idle: Enter an address or hostname and start the trace.
traceroute.incomplete: Stopped after {0} hops without reaching the destination ({1}s)
traceroute.unresolved: {0} could not be resolved to an address.
hop.silentButRouteWorks: This router does not answer traceroute probes - rate limiting, or switched off deliberately. The route itself is fine: hop {0} does answer.
hop.silentTail: No reply from here onwards. Either the path ends here, or everything beyond filters these probes.
hop.silentNearDestination: These routers do not answer probes, but the destination was still reached.
hop.rateLimited: Only {0} of {1} probes answered, while everything after this hop is clean - this router is limiting its own replies, not dropping traffic.
hop.packetLoss: {0}% of probes lost here, and loss continues further along - real packet loss at this point in the route.
hop.netUnreachable: This router has no route to the destination network.
hop.hostUnreachable: This router can reach the network but not the host - it is switched off, or does not exist.
hop.protocolUnreachable: The destination refused the protocol used by the probe.
hop.portUnreachable: The destination was reached; it refused the probe packet, which is a normal end of a trace.
hop.reassemblyTimeout: Fragments of the probe did not arrive in time to be reassembled here.
hop.packetTooBig: The probe was too large for this link and was not forwarded.
hop.loadBalanced: Answers came from {0} different addresses - the traffic is spread across parallel paths.
hop.cgnat: Inside your provider's network, on a shared carrier-grade NAT address.
hop.longHaul: The traffic leaves {0} for {1} here, which is what the extra {2} ms is.
hop.ispPrivateNetwork: Private address space, but not your own LAN - likely inside your provider's internal network.

diagnostics.networkHealth.disabled: Network health monitoring is off - turn it on in Settings.
networkHealth.tcpRetransmissions.what: Your network connection is resending an unusually large number of TCP packets.
networkHealth.tcpRetransmissions.cause: {0} retransmissions in the last {1} minutes usually points to an unstable connection - a poor Wi-Fi signal, an overloaded router, or a problem at the provider.
networkHealth.tcpRetransmissions.todo: Check your Wi-Fi signal strength and cable connections. If this keeps happening, contact your provider.
networkHealth.packetLoss.headline: High packet loss: {0}% in {1} minutes
networkHealth.packetLoss.what: A share of the test packets sent to the internet are not arriving.
networkHealth.packetLoss.cause: An average of {0}% loss over the last {1} minutes points to an unstable connection between this device and the internet.
networkHealth.packetLoss.todo: Check the Wi-Fi connection and cables. If loss stays high, the problem may be with the provider.
networkHealth.ttlExceeded.headline: Many TTL errors: {0} in {1} minutes
networkHealth.ttlExceeded.what: Packets are dying in transit - a router is bouncing them back because their TTL hit zero.
networkHealth.ttlExceeded.cause: {0} TTL errors in the last {1} minutes may point to a routing problem or a TTL set too low. Note: running this app's own traceroute counts toward this as well.
networkHealth.ttlExceeded.todo: Run a traceroute to see where packets are stalling. If this happens outside your own traceroutes, contact your provider.
networkHealth.rogueDhcp.headline: Unexpected DHCP server found ({0})
networkHealth.rogueDhcp.what: A device other than your router is answering DHCP requests on this network.
networkHealth.rogueDhcp.cause: This can be an extra router or access point with DHCP accidentally switched on, or - rarely - a malicious device trying to intercept traffic.
networkHealth.rogueDhcp.todo: Check for an extra router or access point on this network with DHCP enabled, and turn that off. If you do not recognise the device, investigate further.
